Paper · 28 May 2026

Lipid membranes made from scratch without an existing membrane

Khanal, Fracassi, Harjung, Burkart, Devaraj · Nature Communications 17:6920

In a sentence

Vesicles assembled from lipids built out of acetate and cysteine, with no pre-existing membrane to grow from.

In plain words

Every cell membrane today grows from an older membrane, which raises a chicken-and-egg question for the first cell. This team built lipid tails from two simple molecules, acetate and cysteine, using enzymes dissolved in water. The new lipids assembled themselves into bubbles with two-layer walls, and some of these bubbles could hold a difference in acidity between inside and outside.

Technical detail

De novo bilayer formation without pre-existing membranes, membrane proteins or lipid templates. Lipid tails are made by soluble enzymes from acetate and cysteine and form diacyl lipids that assemble into vesicles. Pore-forming peptides let precursors in, so new lipid keeps forming; glycolipid compartments maintain proton gradients. The route uses enzymes, so it is not a prebiotic pathway.

What we take from it

Planned test

Evidence for the lipid-world row and the compartment step of the pathway map. Because it relies on enzymes, we score it as 'shown with biological catalysts', not as a prebiotic step.

Source checked against its DOI. Read the original.
